item.title: How Texas Tech football's CFP ranking surged with 6 teams above losing
item.description: The Texas Tech football team went into the second week of the College Football Playoff rankings with the potential to move up. And move up, it did. The Red Raiders scored a 53-48 home victory against West Virginia last weekend while six teams above them in the initial rankings lost. Tech (8-1, 5-1 in the Big 12) is No. 12 in the new ranking released Tuesday, Nov. 10, up three spots from last week. Were the Red Raiders to remain in that position on selection Sunday, Dec. 6, they would miss the 12-team playoff by one spot. The highest-ranked Group of Six team is guaranteed a spot in the bracket, so Boise State would have the last berth instead of Tech. More: Can we get some answers on this secondary? | Texas Tech football Q&A More: Texas Tech football's Mack Leftwich got first big break under Eric Morris The CFP commences on Dec. 18-19 at campus sites with teams seeded Nos. 5 through 8 hosting teams seeded Nos. 9 through 12. The top four teams this week are Georgia, Utah, Alabama and UCLA. They would receive first-round byes if they hold their spots. Teams ranked 5 through 8, sitting in first-round host positions this week, are Notre Dame, Texas, Miami (Fla.) and Tennessee. The teams slotted 9 through 11 are Indiana, Brigham Young and Kentucky. Texas Tech, Wake Forest, Houston and Iowa are ranked Nos. 12 through 15. The next five are No. 16 Oregon, South Carolina, Southern California, Ole Miss and Ohio State at No. 20. Rounding out the 25 teams are No. 21 LSU, Missouri, Arizona, Boise State and Oklahoma State at No. 25. Tech visits Oklahoma State (6-3, 4-2) in a Big 12 game at 8:30 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 14, at Boone Pickens Stadium in Stillwater. item.title: Damian Lillard is back and Ja Morant is here. How exactly is this going to work? | Bill Oram
item.description: In the history of basketball, we have certainly seen some why-would-they-do-that? pairings. Jerseys and sleeves. Kawhi Leonard and a tree sponsorship. Utah and “the Jazz.” Once, there was even Detlef Schrempf and a headband, if you can believe that. Ja Morant and Damian Lillard? We’re about to find out if they belong on such a list. Because of all the things you might have said the Trail Blazers needed as they prepared to welcome Lillard back after making a playoff run without him, a slight-of-stature ball-dominant guard with a questionable jump shot would not have topped anyone’s list. Depth on the wing? Yes. Shooting? Definitely. Defense? Always. Morant doesn’t particularly address any of those, and yet, he’s here, a dynamic two-time All-Star in need of a second act, being paid a team-high $42.1 million to play the same position as not just Lillard, but Jrue Holiday and Scoot Henderson. Heck, the Blazers’ most valuable point guard last season was forward Deni Avdija. “I’m sure there will be questions about fit,” General Manager Joe Cronin said Monday. Uh, yeah. The Blazers have little more than three weeks before the regular season begins in which to figure that out. At the team’s annual media day on Monday, Morant appeared in a fresh white No. 1 Trail Blazers jersey. It’s happening. “It’s easy for people to be like, ‘Man how is this going to work,’” Lillard offered. “‘They can’t do this, they can’t do that.’ But being on the floor with them … we can be a dangerous team and I really believe that.” The onus is on the Trail Blazers starting this month to prove that they bet right in acquiring Morant. And that pairing him with Lillard isn’t the boondoggle conventional wisdom suggests it will be. Lillard noted how many teams that succeeded in the playoffs last year, think San Antonio with its four point guards, relied on numerous playmakers. To his credit, Morant said he would be comfortable coming off the bench, if necessary. But they would not be the first NBA team to fall into the trap of believing they are capable of adjusting or that they will be comfortable sacrificing. It isn’t uncommon to see players in those situations default to familiar habits and sensibilities once the season is underway or struggles come. That’s what made a lot of the positive energy around what sure seems like an awkward roster ring so hollow. We’re going to need to see it to believe it. Morant tried to lay out a vision for how it could look. If he drives to the paint and is double-teamed, someone else is inevitably open. That’s how basketball works. “That allows me to have more space to be the best Ja I can be,” Morant said. item.title: Oregon star edge rusher Teitum Tuioti out for the season
item.description: EUGENE — One of Oregon football’s most important defensive players is done for the season. Ducks senior defensive end Teitum Tuioti suffered a season-ending knee injury in Oregon’s 41-28 win over Ohio State , Dan Lanning announced on Monday. “Teitum has been unbelievable for us this year, and every year he’s been here,” Lanning said. “Just watching him grow as a player and person has been a lot of fun for us. But unfortunately Teitum’s done for the year, he had a knee injury, he’ll end up having surgery.” Tuioti was among the Ducks’ leaders in tackles with 44, and ranked second on the team in sacks with 5.5 on the season. The former Sheldon High School star sits at No. 8 all-time for Oregon with 22.5 sacks across his four seasons, providing steady leadership on a talented and experienced defensive front. In the win over the Buckeyes, he also showed off his arm: Tuioti completed a pass to fellow defensive end Matayo Uiagalelei on a memorable fake punt which shifted momentum in the game. “I hate it for him, because (the injury) was a routine, weird play that it happened on,” Lanning said. “He left it on the line there on the field, and I don’t know if he’ll get another chance to play as an Oregon football player, but whoever gets to have that guy on their team in the future is gonna be really, really lucky.” Should Tuioti forgo his fifth year of eligibility and enter the NFL Draft, he is a projected second- or third-round pick according to some mock drafts. item.title: Lanning: Stewart incident 'didn't match our standard'
item.description: EUGENE — After Oregon wide receiver Evan Stewart was booked in Springfield Municipal Jail early Sunday morning on DUII charges, Ducks coach Dan Lanning addressed the situation at his weekly press conference Monday. “There was an incident this weekend that didn’t match our standard here in our program,” Lanning said. “There will be an appropriate action taken. Still gathering some details with what that situation looks like. But that would be handled internally. I’m not gonna respond to any other questions about that. We’re gonna handle that with our guys. “There’s an expectation of what you have to... how you have to act, and how you need to perform in our program. Kind of overshadows the success that we had on Saturday, which is disappointing, but that will be handled by us internally. I’m not going to speak on it publicly.” When Lanning was asked a follow-up question about a rumored speeding incident involving other Oregon football players, for which there haven’t been any confirmed arrests, he said, “I was talking about the same thing when I first addressed it.” This is also the second instance of an Oregon football team member facing DUII charges in the past year. In April, running backs coach Ra’Shaad Samples allegedly backed his Ford F-150 into a parked car outside a bar in Eugene. His next court date is Oct. 27. An arraignment for Stewart in his DUII case hasn’t been set, as official charges haven’t been filed to Springfield Municipal Court as of Monday evening, according to court records. Stewart leads the Ducks this season with 27 catches for 352 yards and four touchdowns. He missed Saturday’s win over Nebraska due to an undisclosed injury. Oregon (4-2, 2-1 Big Ten) is preparing for a road game at Illinois (3-3, 1-2) at 12 p.m. PT this coming Saturday. item.title: Who will call plays for Oregon after Mehringer's firing?
item.description: EUGENE — After firing first-year offensive coordinator Drew Mehringer seven games into the 2026 season, Dan Lanning shared Oregon ’s plans for filling his role moving forward at his weekly press conference Monday night. Offensive assistant Jay Johnson will lead offensive playcalling for the Ducks going forward, Lanning said. “He has a lot of experience as a play-caller, was with me in Georgia when we were part of the national championship team,” Lanning said. “Went on to have a lot of success in Colorado and Michigan State. He’s gonna lead the efforts there with the offensive staff, but it’ll still be a collaborative effort, with a lot of the work that we do. “He’s also coming in with a different perspective, a different view, not being with us the last few years, where he can provide a couple things that might be different than what we’ve done.” Mehringer, previously the tight ends coach for the Ducks, is the first assistant coach Lanning has fired in his tenure at Oregon, which began in 2022. The Ducks’ offensive decision-making was at the center of intense criticism over the past three weeks, during which Oregon averaged just 14 points per game and lost twice to UCLA and Illinois. Lanning spoke to the human element of letting Mehringer go. “They see the football coach, right? That’s also an unbelievable dad. A great husband,” Lanning said. “The guy’s been part of our staff for the last five years, that’s done some really good things here, and I think all of us feel like we shoulder some of the blame. item.title: Couch: 3 quick takes on Michigan State basketball's 79-73 win over Duke at the Champions Classic
item.description: 1. As early season statements go, that was a big one by Michigan State CHICAGO — You could see it from the first couple trips up and down the court Tuesday night: Michigan State’s players had a look about them, like guys who’ve been here — in the exhibition season, against Duke last season, in other Champions Classics, and in arenas like this deep into March. And Duke initially looked a little surprised by the Spartans , too. Turned out, it was more than a look. As early season statements go, this was something. The Spartans led wire to wire, taking down a Duke team many think — or thought — might be the best in the country. MSU just joined that conversation on Nov. 10, with a 79-73 win that’ll reverberate throughout college basketball and send expectations for the Spartans soaring. This was a performance that’ll go up there with the most memorable Champions Classic and early season showings by MSU in the Tom Izzo era. It wasn’t how they started but how they held off the Blue Devils when Duke tried to make a run, and how they finished when the Blue Devils cut the deficit to a dicey 73-68 with 2:03 remaining. Jordan Scott responded with the biggest bucket of his career — at least that I can remember — driving to the basket for a layup. A calm play in a moment when calm seemed to be leaving building and all eyes were on how the Spartans would handle the moment. For the most part, they handled the whole night well. Scott had a signature night defensively while only scoring five points. At one point late in the first half, he had as many blocked shots (five) as Duke had made shots. He finished with six blocks — another important one late on a Duke 3-point try — along with nine rebounds and two steals. He was menace of the defensive end. Jeremy Fears Jr.’s stat line might not have matched Denzel Valentine’s triple-down 11 years ago in the Champions Classic, but a similar message was sent in an 18-point, 11-assist, five-round effort, that, while not always the cleanest performance, featured a number of plays when you thought he’s just not going to let MSU lose. Cam Ward (see below), Jasiah Jervis, Carlos Medlock Jr., Coen Carr, and Jesse McCulloch all had games or moments within the game that led to this victory. Maybe Duke isn’t quite what they’re expected to be yet (though the Blue Devils’ exhibition wins say otherwise). Maybe MSU just had a night. Still, when you have a night on this stage, it’s usually real. 2. Cam Ward makes his actual season debut Of all the significant and strong performances by MSU’s players on Tuesday, only one of them was truly a surprise: Cam Ward’s 11 point, five-rebound, one-block night. He finished with 14 points and six rebounds, his bucket at the rim as he was fouled — and ensuing free throw — with 4:59 remaining as important as any play he made all night. item.title: Tony Romo unlikely to appear on Netflix’s Christmas Day NFL doubleheader
item.description: Credit: ESPN Tony Romo reappeared during an NFL game this week, and that’s got a lot of industry people wondering if he might be back on TV screens sooner rather than later. If so, there’s one opportunity in particular that seems ideal. However, one sports media insider has already put the kibosh on that possibility. The former Dallas Cowboys quarterback had essentially been out of sight since being placed on leave and eventually let go from his No. 1 NFL booth role at CBS alongside Jim Nantz following his OWI charge and the subsequent video of his sobriety test that surfaced over the summer. Aside from a few statements and a brief golfing appearance , Romo has been absent from NFL broadcasts this season. But that all changed on Monday night, when Romo joined Pat McAfee’s Monday Night Football ESPN2 altcast via video as the Minnesota Vikings hosted the Buffalo Bills. You’re the man @tonyromo.. Thanks for joining us #PMSMNFonESPN2 https://t.co/YmIf3YZdQH — Pat McAfee (@PatMcAfeeShow) November 10, 2026 Immediately, people started speculating about where Romo might appear next. That includes a sports executive who reached out to Puck’s John Ourand, predicting that he’d show up during Netflix’s Christmas Day NFL doubleheader later this year. Netflix will air two games on Dec. 25: the Green Bay Packers vs. Chicago Bears at Soldier Field, followed by the Buffalo Bills against the Denver Broncos from Empower Field at Mile High. “It seems like a low-risk, high-reward move,” the exec told Ourand. “Plus, everyone loves a comeback story.” That’s true, and it does seem inevitable that Romo will eventually return to our screens in some form, but the sports media insider poured cold water on that specific prediction . “I can say with a good degree of certainty that a Netflix linkup is unlikely to happen for Romo—at least not this season,” said Ourand. As Ourand noted, Monday’s appearance was well orchestrated, with McAfee providing a safe platform for Romo to get back to basics and remind people he’s actually pretty good at analyzing quarterbacks when he’s not making weird noises . As for where Romo shows up next, it’s tough to say. We don’t know if his buyout arrangement with CBS includes any kind of non-compete clause, and if so, for how long. But even if he can work right away, there aren’t many A-booth spots available. Just ask Troy Aikman . If it becomes a buyers’ market, will a network or streamer go with Romo when it can have fresher voices without baggage like Greg Olsen or Sean McVay ? Would he be willing to step down to a B-booth? Or does Romo read the writing on the wall and head to the studio instead? We’ll almost certainly see Tony Romo on NFL programming again soon . But where and in what capacity is anyone’s guess. item.title: CFP rankings: Georgia and Notre Dame move up after big wins
item.description: (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images When the College Football Playoff selection committee released the first set of rankings a week ago, the group not only sparked some controversy, but also teed up a massive Week 10 slate of games. Now that those games are behind us, the rankings look much, much different. Particularly at the top. After debuting at No. 2, Georgia moved up one spot to No. 1, taking the place of Miami. The Bulldogs throttled Ole Miss (who were at No. 10 in the initial rankings) while Miami lost to Notre Dame. Utah moved up as well, as the Utes defeated BYU in a huge Big 12 tilt to maintain an unblemished record and get to No. 2. Miami fell to No. 7 after the loss to Notre Dame. As for the Fighting Irish, the committee gave Notre Dame a clear assignment last week: Beat Miami. With Notre Dame sitting at No. 11 a week ago, another loss likely doomed the Fighting Irish and their playoff hopes. But Notre Dame’s victory at home against the Hurricanes was enough for the committee to move them up to No. 5, and with Notre Dame set to finish the season against three unranked teams, the path is clear for a playoff berth. Alabama at No. 3 and UCLA at No. 4 round out the Top five. Ole Miss fell nine spots after losing. to Georgia. Ohio State fell eight spots after losing to USC. Oklahoma State debuted at No. 25. item.title: ‘Some of the worst officials in America are those in the announce booth’: SEC commissioner blasts media over referee complaints
item.description: Kirby Lee-USA TODAY Sports SEC officiating has come under fire this season, especially after a controversial replay review in the Texas-Missouri game last weekend. But commissioner Greg Sankey isn’t taking the criticism lying down. Sankey defended the conference’s replay process on Monday and took aim at broadcasters who have questioned SEC officials on the air. He said that “some of the worst officials in America are those in the announce booth,” calling one announcer’s criticism “just flat wrong.” SEC Replay Controversy On Saturday, Texas rallied for a 34-20 win at Missouri thanks in part to a baffling call late in the third quarter. Arch Manning was hit as he threw, and the ball sailed forward and hit the turf, but officials ruled it a fumble and Texas recovered for a first down. The call was upheld after a replay review, and the Longhorns scored a game-tying touchdown three plays later. The SEC later explained the ruling , but that didn’t stop the criticism. The SEC has also drawn scrutiny for how it handles replay reviews. The ACC, Big 12, and Big Ten all offer some form of live look-in with audio during replay reviews, but the SEC does not. ‘Just flat wrong’ Appearing on The Paul Finebaum Show on Monday, Sankey explained that the SEC plays as many as seven games at once on Saturdays, making audio access more difficult. He then turned his attention to the people criticizing his officials. “Now I’ll say this: I am highly disappointed in announcers and their criticism. And they’re wrong. Some of the worst officials in America are those in the announce booth,” Sankey said, via On3 . “We have officiating experts, who I turned on a game on Saturday, who was just flat wrong. And what that creates is this narrative that we’ve done something wrong, and that is unacceptable to me, and we have to address that.” Sankey took particular issue with an announcer who weighed in on the Texas-Missouri call during a later game. That broadcast featured Matt Schumacker and Aaron Murray on the call for Florida-Oklahoma. “We’re going to be wrong. We’ve made announcements when we own it. We’re going to have debates about judgment calls,” Sankey said. “But somebody on a Saturday night who’s announcing a game between Oklahoma and Florida going back to something that happened at noon, that he’s never called and asked a question about and being critical is unacceptable in my mind.” “So we’ll take the responsibility, we’ll take the heat, we’ll work to continually improve, we’ll work on how do we provide more transparency and access to a replay system,” he said. The comments came during the same appearance in which Sankey fired back at Big Ten coaches over claims of SEC bias. Clearly, the SEC commissioner wasn’t in the mood to take criticism on Monday. Tigers’ president of baseball operations Scott Harris was asked about the club’s offseason focus and said that they’re prioritizing high leverage relief help that adds swing and miss to the bullpen. The Tigers really have two possible paths to improving a bullpen that was a disaster in high leverage situations in 2026, despite pretty solid numbers overall. item.title: Ugly second half dooms 0-3 Cougs, falling at Duquesne 72-71
item.description: Oct 25, 2025; Pullman, WA, USA; Washington State Cougars head coach David Riley sends in a play against the New Mexico Lobos in the first half at Friel Court at Beasley Coliseum. Mandatory Credit: James Snook-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect A strong first half for the Washington State Cougars was ultimately erased by an ugly, foul-ridden second half as they fell to the Duquesne Dukes 72-71. WSU (0-3) seemed on their way to their first true away victory on the east coast since 1978. With Ronnie Harrison making his debut after missing the first two games of the season, the Cougs played arguably their best first half of the season. They went into the halftime break leading 39-30, shooting 48.1% from the field and outrebounding Duquesne (3-0) 15-14. The second half was a much different story. The Cougs got into foul trouble quickly, putting the Dukes into the bonus just a little over five minutes into the half and into the double bonus before the halfway point in the second half. They finished with 22 total personal fouls. Offensively they cooled off slightly, shooting 42.9% from the field and turned the ball over nine times over the final 20 minutes. Ultimately, the foul trouble that sent the Dukes to the line after every foul five minutes into the second half and caused WSU to play more tentatively on defense overruled the 1.14 points per possession WSU had on offense. With under a minute to play, and the game tied at 69, Sebastian Akins drove through the Duquesne defense and made an incredible finish at the rim through traffic to put WSU in front 71-69 with 32 seconds to go. Now with a two-second difference between the shot and game clock, the Dukes needed to answer. They got their answer from Kerem Konan who drove right at big Mohammed Sankhe standing tall in the paint. Konan went up and through Sankhe for a tough finish that went in and drew a foul to send Konan to the free-throw line for a chance to put the Dukes in front with 12 seconds to play. Konan cashed the go-ahead charity stripe shot. Lazerek Houston was able to get a good look at the buzzer for the game winner, but his shot just missed. This could have been a great early season win for WSU. Going on the road against a solid Duquesne team and a potential quad two victory down the season. Instead, it ended like so many other WSU losses over the past few years. A brutal second half that erased any good feelings of the first 20 minutes of play. In even more unfortunate news, Harrison rerolled his ankle in his WSU debut with 3:39 to play. He was a force on the glass early, grabbing four rebounds, but slowed down as the game went on. He finished with six points, five rebounds and three turnovers. The reigning Pac-12 Freshman of the Week, Jaylen Harrell, again led the way for WSU in points, scoring 19 on 7/10 shooting from the field and splashing a trio of threes. WSU will come home to host Northwest University from the NAIA division at 10am on Saturday.

item.title: College Football Playoff: Kentucky is No. 11 in latest rankings
item.description: Kentucky Football has enjoyed a successful season under first-year head coach Will Stein, as the Wildcats have started the year 7-2 overall and 5-2 in SEC play, putting themselves in College Football Playoff contention, even if they are coming off a 34-6 loss at Tennessee. In the latest CFP rankings unveiled Tuesday night, Kentucky checked in at No. 11, a five-spot drop from last week. Being in the top 11 means the Cats would make the playoff if it began today, but there’s obviously plenty of work left to be done. In addition, FanDuel Sportsbook has Kentucky at +280 to make the playoff, which is tied for the 17th-best odds. Even so, with this ranking, the Wildcats will likely make the playoff if they win out. Far, far, far easier said than done, but the path does exist, a statement few could dream of entering what’s been a special season thus far. When Stein took over the program, not many believed he could turn things around in less than a year. Former head coach Mark Stoops had struggled to close out his tenure in Lexington, posting back-to-back 7-6 seasons in 2022 and 2023, followed by a 4-8 campaign in 2024 and a 5-7 record in 2025 before being fired. Many fans and analysts expected Kentucky to win six games at most this season, while others predicted an even worse finish. However, Stein has exceeded those expectations. The Wildcats have been underdogs in six of their nine games this season, with their only exceptions coming against Youngstown State, South Alabama and Vanderbilt. Despite being underdogs, Stein and Kentucky have won four of those six matchups. Two of those victories came in dramatic fashion, with back-to-back overtime wins against South Carolina on the road and LSU at home. In both games, Kentucky went for two points to seal the victory. Of course, the Wildcats’ two losses as underdogs came against Alabama at home and Tennessee on the road. Unfortunately for Kentucky, both games slipped away in the fourth quarter. Now, the Wildcats have a difficult three-game stretch remaining on their schedule, with Florida at home, Missouri on the road, and Louisville at home. Kentucky will need to win all three games in order to reach the College Football Playoff, which will be no easy task. Although Florida and Louisville have struggled this season, neither opponent can be overlooked. Missouri, meanwhile, has been especially tough to beat at home, with its only home loss coming against Texas this past week. It will be interesting to see how Kentucky responds after its 34-6 loss to Tennessee. However, it is remarkable that Stein has the Wildcats in College Football Playoff contention during his first season, especially with many people viewing this year as a rebuilding campaign. There is still plenty of work to be done, but Stein has already accomplished something few expected when he arrived in Lexington by giving Kentucky a legitimate opportunity to compete for a spot in the College Football Playoff. Let’s ride.

item.description: TRINITY, Texas — Twenty-one years later, Sam Saunders looked around Whispering Pines Golf Club and couldn’t quite get over how much had changed, including his own role. Saunders played in the Spirit International Amateur Golf Championship in 2005. Now 39, retired from professional golf and captain of Team USA, he’s back at Whispering Pines as the event gets underway this week. “And this is my third of these,” Saunders said after Tuesday’s opening ceremony, which is about 90 minutes from Houston. “It’s kind of wild for me that I played in this thing 21 years ago. Pretty much every player on my team was born the year I played. Actually, I think all of them were born the year that I played. It’s weird. “I’m out there feeling like I want to compete with them. But it’s so cool to be back, and this is such a special place.” The Spirit begins Wednesday at the Chet Williams-designed golf course in Trinity, Texas, with 80 of the world’s top amateurs representing 20 countries and six continents. The Olympic-style competition runs through Saturday. For Saunders, it’s a full-circle assignment. He represented the U.S. at the Spirit in 2005 alongside Jamie Lovemark, Amanda McCurdy and Paige Mackenzie, with the Americans finishing tied for second with South Africa. More than two decades later, Saunders has returned to lead four of the country’s top amateurs. His memories of that first Spirit are less about the scores than the experience. “I remember sleeping in a cabin with bunk beds,” Saunders recalled. “I mean, Jamie Lovemark, my teammate, Jason Day was in the bunk bed next to me. It’s just kind of crazy to think back to that time.” That experience remains an important part of the Spirit. Even as elite amateur golf has changed dramatically, especially in the NIL era, players still stay together in cabins at Whispering Pines and spend the week in a setting designed to create relationships beyond the competition. “So many of them are so accomplished,” Saunders said. “In this world of modern sports with NIL and everything, they are living lives that are pretty unique for their age. item.title: Kirk Cousins’ agent due massive payday after Minnesota trade
item.description: Kirk Cousins’ agent, Mike McCartney, has brought the 13-year veteran quarterback some lucrative deals in the past, but with Cousins being traded to the Vikings on Tuesday, the cash flow will continue to pile in from multiple teams. Cousins will spend the rest of the season being paid by the Vikings, Raiders and Falcons. Kirk Cousins celebrating during Sunday’s game against the 49ers. Getty Images During the 2024 offseason, Cousins signed a four-year, $180 million contract with Atlanta and was released from the team last year. Due to a clause in his deal, the Falcons are responsible for paying him $8.7 million this season , and the Raiders will pay a minimum of $1.3 million. The Vikings will pay Cousins about $650,000 for their final nine regular-season games. Before he signed with the Falcons, Cousins spent six seasons with the Vikings and signed a record-breaking $84 million contract that changed the landscape of NFL quarterback contracts in 2018 . Kirk Cousins during Sunday’s press conference after a loss to the 49ers. AP Photo/Justine Willard In 2020, Cousins signed a two-year extension for $66 million, then signed a one-year extension in 2022 for $35 million. While Cousins is set to return to Minnesota, playing for the least amount of money he’s earned in a Vikings uniform, the squad is 6-2 and has one of the NFL’s best defenses. After the Vikings suffered a 23-6 loss to the Bills, in which Carson Wentz completed 8 of 25 passes for 81 yards with two interceptions on Monday night, the Vikings did everything they could to find an answer at quarterback. While Cousins is set for a homecoming in Minnesota, the Raiders will pivot to rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza to try to lead them to the playoffs for the first time since 2021.
